# Education in New Zealand: Key Features
The New Zealand education system is characterized by free, compulsory schooling for all citizens and residents between ages 6 and 16, with most children starting school at age 5 and remaining until at least age 17. The system includes early childhood education, primary (Years 1–8), and secondary (Years 9–13) schooling. Schools are divided by funding type into state (government-funded), state-integrated (retaining a "special character" such as religious affiliation but integrated into the state system), and private schools (independently funded through tuition fees; attended by a small percentage). The school year runs from late January to mid-December, split into four terms, and the curriculum is set nationally, with English-medium and Māori-medium options. The National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA) is the primary qualification for senior students, though some schools also offer Cambridge or International Baccalaureate alternatives.
A significant aspect of New Zealand education is the recognition and revitalization of Māori language and culture. Māori-medium education, including kōhanga reo (preschool), kura kaupapa (primary), and full immersion schools, allows students to learn through Māori for at least 51% of the time, while non-Māori students may access Māori language in English-medium schools. State-integrated schools support diverse religious and educational philosophies, and the system is designed to provide inclusive education, with specialist provisions for students with disabilities. Recent reports show Māori medium students achieving higher outcomes compared to mainstream schooling. School types and structures are varied, including composite and area schools in less populated areas, while the tertiary education sector (post-school) is comprehensively regulated under the New Zealand Qualifications Framework, supporting a unified approach to vocational and university-level education.
